items.text: SEASON 12 · EPISODE 3 · DRAFT · CASE-062  Fenwright Group · month four · Maya, Noor (junior technician), Galen (senior technician), Teodor (head of EMEA, by phone) and Rashida (CIO) · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Late on a Thursday, a regional head wants a firmware fix in every room before his morning board meeting. The instruction travels down: head to senior, senior to junior. It stops at the junior.  ⚑ RV-187: the CIO owns the standard and the change board. RV-189: juniors are backed; reviews are blameless; nothing here is HR advice. RV-188: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: The Junior Who Stopped It
items.stakes: A regional head wants new firmware in every room by morning. The junior on the night rota said no.
items.reward: Eighteen rooms that kept their cameras — and a right to stop that no longer depends on courage.

objectives.text: Decide what Noor should hear from you
Count the rooms it would have reached
Decide how the right to stop survives

items.alt: The lab meeting room at night, its display showing NO SIGNAL; Noor explains, anxious; Maya on the phone, listening.

bubbles.text: Galen told me to push it to all sixty. I put it on the lab room first. The camera's gone.
Tell me exactly what happened to the lab room.

items.caption: One room, not sixty.

lines.text: Galen told me to push it to all sixty. I put it on the lab room first.
Then tell me exactly what happened to the lab room.

items.prompt: 22:50. Noor refused a senior's instruction, and the lab camera is dead. What does she hear from you first?
items.risk: A junior who learns never to say no again.
timeout: Galen calls back and pushes it himself at midnight.

hints.text: What has to be true for Noor to do this again next time?

options.label: “Push it to the other rooms — the lab camera's just old”
options.result: Eighteen more old cameras die before morning.
options.consequence: Overrides the one test that worked.
options.fail: An unapproved change to every room isn't anyone's to make tonight.

options.label: “You did exactly what the standard says. Log what happened; don't touch anything else tonight; I'll find which rooms share that camera and I'll put in writing that you were right”
options.result: Noor logs it at 22:52. By 23:30 Maya has the answer: eighteen rooms carry camera revision A.
options.consequence: Back her first; then the evidence.

options.label: “Why didn't you call me before you did anything?”
options.result: Noor goes quiet. Next time she won't decide anything alone.
options.consequence: Teaches the junior not to use the right she just used.

options.label: “Roll the lab room back and pretend it didn't happen”
options.result: The evidence of eighteen at-risk rooms disappears with it.

items.title: Eighteen rooms.
items.body: The release notes say it on page six: ‘Supported hardware: camera revision B and later.’ The lab room's camera is revision A — and so are the cameras in seventeen other rooms, 18 of 60, including six on the floor where Teodor's board meets at eight. Pushed to all sixty, the firmware would have left thirty percent of the estate without a camera at the most senior hybrid meeting of the quarter.
items.label: Test: the cost of eighteen swaps — and what testing in the lab risked.

items.alt: Sixty squares, one per room: eighteen red squares marked A — camera revision A, which loses its camera if pushed — and forty-two amber, revision B; the lab room outlined. One click to ‘All rooms’: 18 of 60 (30%) dark at the 08:00 board meeting.
items.caption: Thirty percent.

items.title: ‘supported: camera rev. B and later’
items.body: Page six of the release notes, in small print: ‘Supported hardware: camera revision B and later.’ Nobody had read page six. Noor did, at 22:50 — after the lab camera died.

items.title: The cord anyone could pull
items.body: In the middle of the twentieth century, some Japanese car factories hung a cord along the assembly line. Any worker who saw a problem could pull it, and the line would stop until the problem was understood. Managers who came to see it expected chaos. They found that the lines with the cord made fewer defects — because the person closest to the problem was trusted to stop the work.

items.title: One click.
items.body: The management platform's role settings, untouched since installation: a technician may push firmware to one room, a region or ‘All rooms’ — no ticket required. Galen had been rung at home by Teodor and passed the instruction on. On Friday morning he's embarrassed and angry: a junior refused him in front of a regional head. The blameless question isn't who; it's why the most dangerous thing on the platform was also the easiest.
items.label: Test: how long a staged rollout takes — and what the finding was.

items.prompt: Friday, 08:30. Galen is angry and embarrassed. How do you handle him?
items.risk: A senior who stops sharing — or a junior who stops refusing.
timeout: He takes the long way round Noor's desk for a month.

hints.text: What did the system make easy — and what would help Galen say no next time?

options.label: Write him up for giving the instruction
options.result: Galen stops passing on anything — including the things you need to hear.
options.consequence: Blames the messenger for the system.

options.label: Talk to him privately: what pressure he was under, what would have helped — and make the review blameless: the finding is the platform and the missing ticket, not a person
options.result: “Teodor rang me at home. I didn't want to say no to him. I didn't think she'd say no to me.” He pauses. “She was right.”
options.consequence: Respect in private; the system is the finding.

options.label: Say nothing — it all worked out
options.result: Galen and Noor stop speaking to each other.
options.consequence: Leaves a wound and the same one-click tool.

options.label: Tell Teodor it was Galen's fault
options.result: Teodor tells the CIO. The story is now about a person.
options.consequence: Moves the blame up a level.

items.prompt: How does the right to stop survive after this week — and after you leave?
items.risk: The next junior who doesn't dare.

hints.text: What would still protect a junior on a night when you're gone?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S12E03). Option B needs Team at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Thank Noor at the team meeting
options.result: Everyone claps. Nothing is written; the platform is unchanged.

options.label: Stop-work authority written into the standard and signed by Rashida; taught to every technician with the E03 story as the example; the platform changed to need a ticket for more than one room and to roll out in stages
options.result: Rashida signs it on Monday. The platform's ‘All rooms’ button now asks for a ticket number and a stage plan.

options.label: Maya tells each technician personally that they can say no to her
options.consequence: The best you can do without the team's training time — and it leaves with you.

options.label: Ban firmware updates for a year
options.consequence: Removes the risk and adds a worse one.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #114 · AVERY'S LENS  The right to stop is part of the architecture  A junior who can refuse an unapproved change — and be backed for it — protects more rooms than any firmware. Build it into the standard and the tools, not just the culture.  A junior refused to push a firmware update to all sixty rooms at night. It would have killed the camera in eighteen of them.

items.alt: The same sixty squares after the review: forty-two green revision-B rooms staged — lab, three rooms, six rooms, the rest; eighteen grey revision-A rooms held until the vendor fixes the firmware. A ticket, stages and a 24-hour soak each — 72 hours before ‘all’; stop-work authority signed into the standard.

items.title: ‘technician: push to All rooms ✓’
items.body: The management platform's role settings: ‘Technician — may push firmware to: selected room ✓, region ✓, All rooms ✓. Ticket required: ✗.’ Set that way at installation, six years ago.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Every change reaches one room before sixty: read which hardware it supports, get the change approved, lab first, soak, one room per region, a tenth, then all — and record it. Size what a change can reach before you make it. The right to stop only exists when it's written into the standard, built into the tools and backed by leaders when a junior uses it — and the review asks what the system made easy, not who to blame.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Who in your team could stop you — and would they?
